text: hey everybody a famous passage from Latter-Day Saints scripture is the book of Mormon's book of second Nephi chapter
25 verse 23 where at the end it says we know that it is by grace that we are saved after all we can do and this
passage has long been interpreted by both Latter-Day Saints and by others as a reference to a works-based Salvation
the notion that Grace only kicks in once we have exhausted all of our efforts and done all that we can do
but this is a misreading this is not what the author intended the hearer or the reader to understand by this statement when this passage was written
whoever its author was the intended sense was it is by grace that we are saved despite all we can do
to demonstrate this I published a paper in the journal Book of Mormon studies in 2020 where I looked at occurrences of
this phrase after all we he she they can do and I demonstrated that across all
its usage it always occurred in contexts that demanded the understanding despite
all we she they can do now I looked at all the examples of this construction I could find in literature from the 18th
and the early 19th centuries and I couldn't find a single occurrence where the sense was clearly subsequent to all
we can do rather than despite all we can do and interestingly enough this construction was frequently used precisely in discussions about Grace
reflecting the idea that we get from Luke and that we also find in the Book of Mormon that we are unprofitable
servants even if we do everything that we are told to do so the reading despite all we can do is consistent with the
book of Mormon's conceptual is of grace and the works-based reading the notion that Grace only kicks in after we have
exhausted all of our efforts is a Latter-day Saint renegotiation of what the Book of Mormon originally meant
